population: 697 patients with peripheral clinical T1aN0M0 NSCLC ≤2 cm with pathologically confirmed node-negative disease
benefitText: Five-year disease-free survival was 63.6% after sublobar resection versus 64.1% after lobectomy. Sublobar resection met the prespecified non-inferiority criterion. Five-year overall survival was 80.3% vs 78.9% (HR for death 0.95, 95% CI 0.72–1.26).
harmText: At 6 months, the median percentage of predicted FEV1 was about 2 percentage points better after sublobar resection; no single toxicity endpoint supports a defensible NNH.
clinicalInterpretation: For carefully selected peripheral ≤2-cm node-negative stage IA NSCLC, sublobar resection provides disease control and survival comparable to lobectomy while preserving more lung function. The result is a non-inferiority finding, not evidence that sublobar surgery improves survival.
clinicalQuestion: In peripheral stage IA NSCLC ≤2 cm, can sublobar resection replace lobectomy without compromising cancer control?
refs: Altorki NK, et al. N Engl J Med. 2023;388:489–498.

treatment: Consolidation durvalumab after concurrent chemoradiotherapy vs placebo
population: 713 patients with unresectable stage III NSCLC without progression after concurrent chemoradiotherapy
relativeEffect: 0.72 for overall survival; 0.55 for progression-free survival
benefitText: Five-year overall survival was 42.9% with durvalumab versus 33.4% with placebo, an absolute improvement of 9.5 percentage points (NNT 11). Five-year PFS was 33.1% vs 19.0%, an absolute improvement of 14.1 points.
harmLabel: Treatment discontinuation because of adverse events
nnH: 18, based on treatment discontinuation due to adverse events
harmText: Treatment discontinuation because of adverse events occurred in 15.4% with durvalumab versus 9.8% with placebo. Grade 3–4 adverse events were 30.5% vs 26.1%.
clinicalInterpretation: PACIFIC established the consolidation paradigm in unresectable stage III NSCLC: after successful definitive CRT, one year of durvalumab produces a durable 9.5-point absolute 5-year survival gain. This provides the critical comparator for understanding why the same conceptual strategy did not succeed after SBRT in S1914.
clinicalQuestion: After definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy for unresectable stage III NSCLC, does consolidation durvalumab improve survival?
refs: Spigel DR, et al. J Clin Oncol. 2022;40:1301–1311.

treatment: Neoadjuvant weekly carboplatin/paclitaxel with concurrent radiotherapy followed by surgery vs surgery alone
population: 368 patients with resectable esophageal or gastroesophageal-junction cancer
benefitText: Five-year overall survival was 47% after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy plus surgery versus 34% after surgery alone, an absolute improvement of 13 percentage points (NNT 8). R0 resection was 92% vs 69%.
harmText: No reliable fixed-time excess in a single clinically dominant severe-toxicity endpoint supports an NNH; postoperative complications and in-hospital mortality were broadly similar.
clinicalInterpretation: CROSS established that preoperative chemoradiotherapy can produce a large survival gain and substantially improve R0 resection in locally advanced esophageal/GEJ cancer. It is the foundational upper-GI trimodality trial for subsequent intensification and immunotherapy strategies.
clinicalQuestion: In resectable locally advanced esophageal or GEJ cancer, does neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by surgery improve survival over surgery alone?
refs: Shapiro J, et al. Lancet Oncol. 2015;16:1090–1098.

population: 716 patients with resectable gastric or gastroesophageal-junction adenocarcinoma
benefitText: Five-year overall survival was approximately 45% with perioperative FLOT versus 36% with ECF/ECX, an absolute improvement of about 9 percentage points (NNT 12). Median overall survival was 50 vs 35 months.
nnH: Not quantifiable from a single trial-specific dominant toxicity endpoint
harmText: FLOT increases treatment intensity and specific toxicities such as neutropenia and diarrhoea; the overall grade 3–4 toxicity burden was substantial in both groups.
clinicalInterpretation: FLOT4 established a more effective perioperative chemotherapy backbone for resectable gastric/GEJ adenocarcinoma. The survival gain is clinically meaningful but must be weighed against the greater intensity and toxicity of FLOT.
clinicalQuestion: In resectable gastric or GEJ adenocarcinoma, does perioperative FLOT improve survival compared with older ECF/ECX chemotherapy?

treatment: Radiotherapy plus concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide vs radiotherapy alone
population: 573 adults with newly diagnosed glioblastoma or gliosarcoma after surgery
benefitText: Two-year survival increased from 10.4% with radiotherapy alone to 26.5% with radiotherapy plus concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide, an absolute improvement of 16.1 percentage points (NNT 7). Median OS was 14.6 vs 12.1 months.
harmText: Grade 3–4 haematologic toxicity during chemoradiotherapy occurred in about 7% with temozolomide versus 0% with radiotherapy alone.
clinicalInterpretation: The Stupp regimen transformed postoperative glioblastoma treatment: approximately one additional patient was alive at two years for every seven treated, with a relatively modest severe-haematologic toxicity burden.
clinicalQuestion: Does adding concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide to postoperative radiotherapy improve survival in newly diagnosed glioblastoma?
refs: Stupp R, et al. N Engl J Med. 2005;352:987–996.

treatment: Radiotherapy followed by 12 cycles adjuvant temozolomide vs radiotherapy without adjuvant temozolomide
population: 444 adults with newly diagnosed IDH-mutant, 1p/19q non-codeleted grade 3 astrocytoma within the molecularly defined CATNON population
benefitText: In IDH-mutant tumours, median overall survival was 12.5 years with adjuvant temozolomide versus 6.0 years without adjuvant temozolomide; HR 0.54 (95% CI 0.42–0.69; P<.0001). Concurrent temozolomide did not significantly improve OS (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.63–1.04).
nnt: Not quantifiable for the mature median-survival endpoint; the absolute effect is best expressed by the 6.5-year difference in median OS.
relativeEffect: 0.54 for adjuvant TMZ in IDH-mutant tumours
harmText: The final publication did not report a single fixed-time toxicity endpoint suitable for a defensible NNH; treatment burden should therefore be described directly.
clinicalInterpretation: CATNON separates the value of concurrent from adjuvant temozolomide. In IDH-mutant grade 3 astrocytoma, the durable survival benefit is driven by adjuvant TMZ after radiotherapy, not by adding TMZ concurrently during radiotherapy.
clinicalQuestion: In newly diagnosed IDH-mutant, 1p/19q non-codeleted grade 3 astrocytoma, does adjuvant temozolomide improve survival, and does concurrent temozolomide add benefit?
refs: van den Bent MJ, et al. Lancet Oncol. CATNON final molecular/clinical analysis; median follow-up 10.9 years.

setting: Adjuvant · Stage III / High-Risk Stage II
population: 2246 patients with completely resected stage II or III colon cancer
relativeEffect: 0.80 for disease-free survival in stage II/III overall population
ci: 95% CI approximately 0.68–0.93 in the long-term analysis
benefitText: Five-year disease-free survival was 73.3% with FOLFOX4 versus 67.4% with LV5FU2, an absolute improvement of 5.9 percentage points (NNT 17). Six-year OS was 78.5% vs 76.0% overall; in stage III disease it was 72.9% vs 68.7%.
harmText: Grade 3 sensory neuropathy was substantially more frequent with oxaliplatin-containing therapy; neuropathy is the defining treatment-burden trade-off of adding oxaliplatin.
clinicalInterpretation: MOSAIC established the survival-relevant benefit of adding oxaliplatin to fluoropyrimidine adjuvant therapy, while also making cumulative neuropathy an explicit part of the benefit–harm calculation that later duration trials refine.
clinicalQuestion: In resected stage II/III colon cancer, does adding oxaliplatin to fluoropyrimidine improve disease control and survival?
refs: André T, et al. J Clin Oncol. 2009;27:3109–3116.

setting: Locally Advanced Disease · Total Neoadjuvant Therapy
treatment: Short-course radiotherapy followed by chemotherapy and surgery vs standard long-course chemoradiotherapy followed by surgery and optional adjuvant chemotherapy
population: 920 patients with high-risk locally advanced rectal cancer
benefitText: Three-year disease-related treatment failure was 23.7% with the RAPIDO strategy versus 30.4% with standard treatment, an absolute reduction of 6.7 percentage points (NNT 15). pCR was approximately 28% vs 14%.
harmText: Grade ≥3 diarrhoea was approximately 18% with the experimental strategy versus 9% with standard chemoradiotherapy. Long-term local-control trade-offs and subsequent treatment exposure remain clinically important.
clinicalInterpretation: RAPIDO established that a short-course RT/TNT strategy can reduce early disease-related treatment failure, but the absolute gain should not be interpreted as an overall-survival benefit. Later follow-up highlights the importance of balancing distant control against local recurrence risk and treatment burden.
clinicalQuestion: In high-risk locally advanced rectal cancer, can short-course RT followed by systemic chemotherapy reduce treatment failure compared with conventional chemoradiotherapy?
refs: Bahadoer RR, et al. Lancet Oncol. 2021;22:29–42.

treatment: Modified FOLFIRINOX vs gemcitabine after resection
population: 493 patients with resected pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
benefitText: Five-year overall survival was 43.2% with modified FOLFIRINOX versus 31.4% with gemcitabine, an absolute improvement of 11.8 percentage points (NNT 9). Five-year disease-free survival was 26.1% vs 19.0%.
harmText: Grade 3–4 adverse events occurred in 75.9% with modified FOLFIRINOX versus 51.9% with gemcitabine. Grade 3–4 diarrhoea and sensory neuropathy were important regimen-specific burdens.
clinicalInterpretation: PRODIGE 24 is one of the clearest Absolute Effect examples: approximately 12 additional survivors per 100 patients at five years, at the price of markedly greater treatment toxicity. The magnitude of benefit makes intensity worthwhile for fit patients, but regimen tolerance is central to patient selection.
clinicalQuestion: After pancreatic resection, does modified FOLFIRINOX improve survival compared with gemcitabine?
refs: Conroy T, et al. JAMA Oncol. 2022;8:1263–1270.

treatment: Neoadjuvant gemcitabine-based chemoradiotherapy followed by surgery and adjuvant gemcitabine vs upfront surgery and adjuvant gemcitabine
population: 246 patients with resectable or borderline-resectable pancreatic cancer
benefitText: Five-year overall survival was 20.5% after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy versus 6.5% with upfront surgery, an absolute improvement of 14 percentage points (NNT 8). R0 resection was 71% vs 40% among resected patients.
harmText: Serious adverse events were reported more often during the neoadjuvant treatment phase, but no single fixed-time toxicity endpoint provides a sufficiently clean basis for a defensible NNH.
clinicalInterpretation: PREOPANC provides randomized evidence that treating pancreatic cancer before surgery can improve long-term survival and R0 resection. The large absolute 5-year survival difference supports the neoadjuvant concept, while contemporary practice must now consider whether modern systemic chemotherapy can produce greater benefit with less radiotherapy burden.
clinicalQuestion: In resectable or borderline-resectable pancreatic cancer, does neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy improve survival compared with immediate surgery?
refs: Versteijne E, et al. J Clin Oncol. 2022;40:1220–1230.
